los.description: Explain the geometric meaning of vectors, dot products, norms, projections and matrix products, given two- and three-dimensional examples
Describe what rank, eigenvalues and singular values reveal about a matrix and name one machine learning use of each, given covariance and data matrices
Identify ill-conditioned or rank-deficient systems and explain their effect on a least-squares fit, given five numerical cases
Compute products, inverses, projections and decompositions by hand for small matrices and in array code for large ones, given the weekly problem sets
Implement least squares through QR factorisation and compare it with the normal equations, given synthetic data with nearly collinear features
Apply the singular value decomposition to build low-rank approximations and principal components, given a public image, ratings or embedding matrix

questions.prompt: Learners are vectors of (video minutes, quizzes). Learner K is (300, 2). Which is nearest to K by Euclidean distance: M (305, 9), N (330, 2) or P (290, 2)?
options: P, because it matches K exactly on quizzes
N, because its only difference is in one coordinate
M, at a distance of about 8.6
None: minutes and quizzes cannot be combined in one distance
questions.explanation: M: √(5² + 7²) ≈ 8.6; P: 10; N: 30. M wins although it took seven more quizzes, because one quiz counts as much as one minute here. Whether that is sensible is a scaling decision.
misconceptions: Takes a perfect match on one coordinate as closeness: P is still 10 minutes away, more than M's distance
Counts how many coordinates differ instead of how far: N's one difference is 30 minutes, the largest gap of the three
Believes a distance cannot be computed across units: it can, but its meaning depends on the scales chosen

questions.prompt: A question vector q = (1, 1). Two help articles: A = (4, 4) and B = (1, 1.2). Which statement is right?
options: A is closer in direction, since q · A = 8 beats q · B = 2.2
A and q differ in direction, since A is four times longer
Both measures rank A first, so the choice never matters
A has cosine 1 with q and B a little less; the dot product also rewards A's length
questions.explanation: A = 4q, so cos(q, A) = 1; B is slightly off q's direction. Both measures put A first here, for different reasons.
misconceptions: Takes the larger dot product as the closer direction: A wins on dot product only because it is longer
Treats different lengths as different directions: A is exactly four times q
Assumes cosine and dot product always rank the same way: they agree only when all vectors have equal length

questions.prompt: A search over mean word vectors returns two articles with cosines 0.951 and 0.949 to a question. What is the soundest reading?
options: The scores barely differ; check whether a shared direction inflates every cosine before trusting the order
Both are excellent matches, since a cosine above 0.9 means near-identical meaning
The first article is clearly the better answer, since it scores higher
There is a 95% chance that either article answers the question
questions.explanation: High, nearly equal cosines are what a shared direction produces. Centring the vectors and comparing again shows whether the order means anything.
misconceptions: Reads a high cosine as a strong match: when all vectors share a direction, every cosine is high
Treats a small gap in a high-dimensional score as a clear ranking: distances concentrate
Confuses cosine with a probability: a cosine is an angle measure, not a chance

questions.prompt: Three vectors: a = (2, 0), b = (10, 1), c = (1, 1). Which pair has the largest cosine similarity?
options: a and b, because their dot product, 20, is the largest
a and b, at a cosine of about 0.995
a and c, because they have similar lengths
b and c, because both have a second coordinate of 1
misconceptions: Ranks by dot product, which rewards b's length: a · b = 20 is large only because b is long
Assumes vectors of similar length are similar in direction: c is at 45° from a
Reads the shared second coordinate as shared direction: b points mostly along the first axis

questions.prompt: A layer compares 12 queries with 30 keys, each vector of length 64. What is the shape of S = Q Kᵀ?
questions.explanation: Q is 12 × 64 and Kᵀ is 64 × 30; the inner 64 is summed in each dot product, leaving one score per query and key.
misconceptions: Multiplies in the wrong order: K Qᵀ would be 30 × 12
Keeps the vector length as a dimension: the dot product sums it away
Thinks a product keeps the inner size: in (12 × 64)(64 × 30) the 64 disappears

questions.prompt: S doubles every vector's first coordinate; T turns the plane a quarter turn. You want one matrix that scales first, then turns. Which is it?
options: T S
S T
S + T
S T or T S, which are equal
questions.explanation: (T S) x = T (S x): S acts on x first, then T acts on the result.
misconceptions: Reads a product left to right like a sentence: the right-hand matrix acts first
Adds maps instead of composing them: S + T is neither map
Thinks the order of matrices never changes the result: here S T and T S differ

questions.prompt: Multiplying two 500 × 500 matrices takes 0.25 GFLOPs. About how many FLOPs does a 1,000 × 1,000 product take?
options: 0.5 GFLOPs
1 GFLOP
4 GFLOPs
2 GFLOPs
questions.explanation: 2n³: doubling n multiplies n³ by 8, and 8 × 0.25 = 2.
misconceptions: Scales the cost with n: the cost grows with n³
Scales the cost with the number of entries, n²: each entry also grows longer
Scales with n⁴, counting the entries twice

questions.prompt: A is 100 × 2,000, B is 2,000 × 2,000 and x is a vector of length 2,000. You need A B x. Which order costs fewer FLOPs?
options: Either: the answer is the same, so the cost is the same
(A B) x
A (B x)
Whichever order NumPy chooses, since it optimises the brackets
questions.explanation: B x costs 8 million FLOPs and A(Bx) 0.4 million more; (A B) alone costs 800 million.
misconceptions: Thinks the cost is fixed by the result: the result is the same, the work is not
Multiplies the matrices first by habit: (A B) costs 2·100·2,000·2,000 = 800 million FLOPs
Believes a library reorders the brackets for you: NumPy computes them in the order written

questions.prompt: A table has columns: price, tax (15% of price), price with tax, and a discount code that varies freely. What is its rank, if there are many rows?
questions.explanation: Tax = 0.15 × price and price with tax = 1.15 × price: both lie on price's direction. Price and the discount code are independent.
misconceptions: Counts columns, not independent columns: tax and price with tax follow from price
Misses that tax depends on price: only price with tax repeats the others
Thinks a column computed from another removes both: price still carries its own direction

questions.prompt: Elimination on a 4 × 4 matrix finds no non-zero pivot in the third column, even after looking for a row to swap. What follows?
options: The computation needs more precision
The system has exactly one solution, found by skipping the column
The columns are dependent; the system has no solution or infinitely many
The right-hand side b must be zero
questions.explanation: A missing pivot means a column is a combination of earlier ones: rank below 4, a singular matrix.
misconceptions: Believes a bigger computer fixes it: the zero is structural, not a rounding accident
Assumes a solution exists and is unique: a dependent column removes uniqueness
Confuses a zero pivot with a zero right-hand side: b plays no part in the pivots

questions.prompt: A 3 × 3 matrix has rows (1, 2, 3), (0, 1, 4) and (1, 3, 7). Does it have an inverse?
options: Yes: no row is all zeros
Yes: no two rows are equal
It depends on the vector b it is used with
No: the third row is the sum of the first two
questions.explanation: (1, 2, 3) + (0, 1, 4) = (1, 3, 7). Rank 2: the map squashes a direction, so it cannot be undone.
misconceptions: Thinks a matrix with no zero row is invertible: rows can depend on each other without being zero
Looks only for equal rows: dependence can be any combination
Thinks invertibility depends on the right-hand side: it is a property of the matrix alone

questions.prompt: A 1,000 × 6 table of features has rank 5. What can you conclude?
options: Five of the 1,000 rows are independent, the rest repeat them
One column has missing values
One column is a combination of the others; a model cannot separate all six effects
The sixth column must be deleted
questions.explanation: Six columns but only five independent directions: some non-zero combination of columns is zero.
misconceptions: Thinks rank counts rows: it is at most the smaller of rows and columns, here 6
Thinks a lower rank means a missing value: rank is about combinations, not gaps
Thinks the last column is the culprit: any one of the dependent columns could be removed

questions.prompt: Project b = (4, 2) onto the line through a = (1, 0). Which is the projection, and why?
options: (0, 2), the part along the second axis
(4, 0), since b · a / a · a = 4
(4), the number b · a
(0.894, 0), the unit vector of b on the axis
questions.explanation: b · a = 4 and a · a = 1, so p = 4a = (4, 0); the residual (0, 2) is orthogonal to the line.
misconceptions: Projects onto the other axis: the line through (1, 0) is the first axis
Returns the coefficient as if it were the point: 4 is a length along a, the point is 4a
Normalises b instead of projecting it: the projection keeps the shadow's length

questions.prompt: Your function returns Q (5 × 3) and R (3 × 3) for a 5 × 3 matrix A. Which set of checks is enough?
options: QᵀQ = I
Q R = A
Q equals np.linalg.qr(A)[0] entry by entry
QᵀQ = I, Q R = A and R upper triangular
questions.explanation: Together they define a QR factorisation; each alone admits wrong answers.
misconceptions: Checks only one of the two properties: an orthonormal Q of the wrong span passes
Checks the product only: Q R = A also holds for Q = A and R = I
Compares with the library entry by entry: correct factorisations can differ in sign

questions.prompt: For a QR of a feature matrix you measure max |QᵀQ − I| = 0.02. What is the soundest next step?
options: Suspect nearly dependent columns, check the condition number, and use a Householder QR
Accept it: 0.02 is a small number
Use fewer rows so the factorisation is faster and more accurate
Normalise each column of Q again to length 1
questions.explanation: A loss of 0.02 is about 10¹⁴ times rounding level: the columns are nearly dependent, and the method in use (typically classical Gram-Schmidt) does not keep Q orthonormal.
misconceptions: Treats 0.02 as negligible: in float64 a sound Q is within about 1e-15
Blames the size of the data: orthogonality loss comes from the angles between columns
Thinks normalising fixes orthogonality: unit length says nothing about the angles between columns

questions.prompt: P projects onto the span of the columns of A, and r = v − P v. Which statement always holds?
options: P has an inverse
P r = r
Aᵀ r = 0
questions.explanation: The residual of an orthogonal projection is orthogonal to every column; in fact P r = 0.
misconceptions: Confuses orthogonal with equal length: the residual can be any length
Thinks a projection matrix is invertible: it squashes the orthogonal directions to zero
Applies P to the residual and expects r back: the residual has no part in the subspace

questions.prompt: Two candidate fits for the same data. Fit F has residual (1, −2, 1) and fit G has residual (2, −1, −1). The columns of X are (1, 1, 1) and (−1, 0, 1). Which can be the least-squares fit?
options: G, because its residual is more even
F, because its residual is orthogonal to both columns
Both, since their residuals have the same length
Neither, because neither residual is zero
misconceptions: Judges a residual by how even its entries look: what decides is orthogonality to the columns
Thinks equal norms mean both are optimal: the least-squares residual is unique
Believes a non-zero residual means no fit is least squares: least squares rarely reaches zero

questions.prompt: A fit has cond(X) = 10⁷. Refitting after rounding the data to four decimals changes two coefficients by 30% and the fitted values by 0.01%. What is the diagnosis?
options: The rounding was too coarse; the model is fine
The model is stable, since its predictions hardly moved
Ill-conditioned: nearly collinear columns; trust the fit, not those two coefficients
Rank-deficient: one column must be removed before any fit
questions.explanation: Full rank, high condition number, stable predictions, unstable coefficients: the pattern of near-collinearity.
misconceptions: Blames the rounding: rounding only revealed a sensitivity that was already there
Reads stable predictions as stable coefficients: the two can differ
Calls any large condition number rank-deficient: the rank is still full

questions.prompt: A feature matrix has cond(X) = 10⁶ in float64. You need coefficients accurate to at least six digits. Which route?
options: The normal equations: they are fastest
QR, which puts about 6 digits at risk and leaves about 10
The normal equations in float32 to save memory
Invert XᵀX and multiply by Xᵀy
questions.explanation: QR works with cond(X) = 10⁶: about 16 − 6 = 10 digits remain.
misconceptions: Ignores the squaring: cond(XᵀX) = 10¹² leaves about 4 digits
Thinks float32 speeds things up harmlessly: it carries only about 7 digits
Inverts XᵀX instead of solving: the conditioning is the same or worse

questions.prompt: A model fitted by the normal equations and by QR gives coefficients that differ in the third significant digit. The residual norms agree to eight digits. What is the most likely cause?
options: Nearly collinear columns: cond(X) is high and the normal equations square it
A bug in the QR routine of the library
Nothing: equal residuals mean the coefficients must be equal too
Too few rows; more data would make the methods agree
questions.explanation: Stable residuals with unstable coefficients is the signature of near-collinearity, amplified by forming XᵀX.
misconceptions: Blames the solver for a bug: two correct methods disagree exactly where the problem is ill-conditioned
Thinks equal residuals prove equal coefficients: many β give nearly the same fit
Takes the sample size as the cause: conditioning is about the columns' angles

questions.prompt: A symmetric 3 × 3 matrix has eigenvalues 9, 4 and 0. Which statement is right?
options: Its diagonal entries are 9, 4 and 0
It is invertible, because two eigenvalues are positive
It has rank 2 and squashes one direction to zero
Its eigenvectors have lengths 9, 4 and 0
questions.explanation: A v = 0 for the eigenvector of 0: that direction is lost, so the rank is 2 and there is no inverse.
misconceptions: Thinks eigenvalues are diagonal entries: they are only for a diagonal matrix
Believes a zero eigenvalue only means a small entry: it means a direction sent to zero
Confuses symmetric with orthogonal: an orthogonal matrix keeps lengths, eigenvalues of size 1

questions.prompt: Four features of course pages have a covariance matrix with eigenvalues 30, 5, 1 and 0.5. What can you say?
options: All four features carry about the same information
About 82% of the variance lies along one direction, a combination of the features
The first feature explains 82% of the variance
The fourth feature is an error and must be removed
questions.explanation: 30 / (30 + 5 + 1 + 0.5) ≈ 0.82, along the leading eigenvector, which mixes the features.
misconceptions: Equates the number of eigenvalues with the number of useful features: the spread is uneven
Thinks a component is one of the original features: it is a combination of all four
Reads the smallest eigenvalue as an error: a small variance is still variance

questions.prompt: With damping d = 0.85, power iteration converges in about a hundred steps; at d = 0.99 it takes many more. Why?
options: A larger d removes pages from the graph
A larger d makes the leading eigenvalue larger than 1
A larger d needs a better starting vector
The second-largest eigenvalue is at most d, so the error shrinks more slowly when d is near 1
questions.explanation: The error shrinks by about |λ₂| per step, and |λ₂| ≤ d: 0.99 shrinks it by only 1% a step.
misconceptions: Thinks larger d means fewer pages: the graph is the same
Thinks the leading eigenvalue changes: it stays exactly 1
Thinks convergence depends on the starting vector only: the eigenvalue gap governs it

questions.prompt: You repeat x ← A x / ‖A x‖ for a symmetric A with eigenvalues 7, 3 and −2, from a random start. What does x approach?
options: The eigenvector of −2
The eigenvector of 7, up to sign
An average of the three eigenvectors
Nothing: dividing by the norm each step prevents convergence
questions.explanation: The part along the eigenvector of 7 grows by 7 each step, the others by at most 3: the ratio 3/7 shrinks them away.
misconceptions: Picks the eigenvalue with the largest index: power iteration picks the largest size
Thinks the iteration averages the eigenvectors: the largest one outgrows the rest
Thinks normalising stops convergence: it only keeps the numbers in range

questions.prompt: A 500 × 40 feature matrix has singular values 310, 52, 9, … , 0.004, 0.000002. What does that tell you?
options: All 40 directions are equally informative
The condition number is 310
Full rank but nearly rank-deficient: cond ≈ 1.6 × 10⁸, unsafe for the normal equations
The rank is 3
questions.explanation: 310 / 0.000002 = 1.55 × 10⁸; squared, it reaches the limit of float64.
misconceptions: Treats every non-zero σ as equally important: tiny ones are close to dependence
Reads the largest σ as the condition number: it is the ratio of largest to smallest
Counts only σ above 1 as the rank: rank counts all non-zero values

questions.prompt: A matrix has singular values 10, 6, 3 and 1. What is ‖A − A₂‖_F, the error of its best rank-2 approximation?
questions.explanation: √(3² + 1²) = √10: the square root of the sum of the squares of the dropped singular values.
misconceptions: Takes the next singular value alone: the Frobenius error includes every dropped one
Adds the dropped values without squaring: the Frobenius norm adds squares
Uses the kept values instead of the dropped ones

questions.prompt: A colleague takes the SVD of a ratings matrix without centring it. The first singular value is huge and the first right singular vector has nearly equal entries. What happened?
options: The first layer captures the average rating, not a pattern of variation
Every item is rated the same by every person
The matrix has rank 1
The SVD routine has failed
questions.explanation: Without centring, the mean is the largest common direction; PCA needs the spread around the mean.
misconceptions: Thinks equal entries mean the items are identical: they share a mean, not a pattern
Thinks a large σ₁ means the matrix has rank 1: other σ can still be large
Blames the library: the SVD of an uncentred matrix is correct, just answering another question

questions.prompt: A 600 × 400 image has singular values that fall slowly: rank 300 still leaves 5% relative error. What should you conclude?
options: A rank-300 copy is a good way to save space
The SVD was computed wrongly
This image has little low-rank structure; truncation is a poor compressor for it
Centring the image would make rank 10 enough
questions.explanation: Storage k(m + n + 1) exceeds m n from k = 240, and the error is still 5%: the singular values decide.
misconceptions: Assumes any truncation saves space: a rank-300 copy stores 300 × 1,001 numbers, more than 240,000
Thinks the SVD failed: slow decay is a property of the image
Thinks centring always makes a matrix low-rank: it removes one layer at most

questions.prompt: Held-out errors for ranks 1 to 6 of a film-ratings model: 0.91, 0.86, 0.84, 0.85, 0.87, 0.90. Training errors fall from 0.88 to 0.61. Which rank?
options: 6, with the lowest training error
3, with the lowest held-out error
1, the simplest model
4, the middle of the range
questions.explanation: Held-out error is lowest at rank 3 and rises after: later layers fit noise.
misconceptions: Chooses by training error, which always favours the largest rank
Picks the smallest model by habit: rank 1 is clearly worse on held-out data
Averages ranks instead of comparing errors: the average has no meaning here

questions.prompt: X has shape (100, 5). What does X - X.mean(axis=0) do?
options: Subtracts each row's mean from that row
Raises a shape error
Subtracts one overall mean from every entry
Subtracts each column's mean from that column
questions.explanation: X.mean(axis=0) has shape (5,); it lines up with the last dimension and stretches over the 100 rows.
misconceptions: Confuses axis 0 with rows: axis=0 averages down the rows, one mean per column
Expects an error: shapes (100, 5) and (5,) line up from the right
Thinks the mean is a single number: axis=0 gives one per column

questions.prompt: A test asserts Q.T @ Q == np.eye(3) for a correct QR and fails. What is wrong?
options: Exact equality on floats: compare with a tolerance instead
The QR routine has a bug
The product should be Q @ Q.T
Convert Q to float32 first
questions.explanation: Entries differ from 0 and 1 by about 10⁻¹⁶: correct, but not exactly equal.
misconceptions: Blames the factorisation: a correct Q is orthonormal only up to rounding
Thinks Q.T @ Q needs a different order: Q Qᵀ is not the identity for a tall Q
Believes float32 would fix it: fewer digits make the gap larger

questions.prompt: Two help articles are represented by the vectors a = (3, 4) and b = (4, 3). What is their cosine similarity?
questions.explanation: a · b = 24 and ‖a‖ = ‖b‖ = 5, so the cosine is 24 / 25 = 0.96.
misconceptions: Takes the raw dot product as the similarity, ignoring the vectors' lengths
Divides by ‖a‖² + ‖b‖² instead of by ‖a‖ · ‖b‖
Compares one pair of components (3 / 4) instead of the whole vectors

questions.prompt: Every article vector in a search index has a large shared component, and almost every pair of articles has a cosine near 0.85. What does subtracting the mean vector before comparing do?
options: It makes every vector length 1, so cosines become dot products
It removes the direction every vector shares, so the cosine compares how articles differ
It leaves the cosines unchanged, because cosine already ignores length
It makes every cosine exactly 0
questions.explanation: Cosine ignores length but not a shared offset; centring removes the common direction, so similarities reflect differences between articles.
misconceptions: Confuses centring with normalising to unit length
Thinks cosine ignores a shared offset; it ignores scale, not translation
Expects centring to make all vectors orthogonal; it only removes their mean

questions.prompt: Attention scores are the product Q Kᵀ, where Q and K are both 1,024 × 64. Counting a multiply and an add as two operations, about how many floating-point operations does it take?
options: About 67 million
About 8.4 million
About 1 million
questions.explanation: The result has 1,024 × 1,024 entries and each is a 64-term dot product: 64 multiplies and 64 adds.
misconceptions: Counts only the multiplications, not the additions
Computes the 64 × 64 product Kᵀ Q, a different matrix (2 × 64 × 64 × 1,024)
Counts the entries of the result, not the work for each entry

questions.prompt: Project y = (2, 3) onto the line through u = (1, 1). What is the projection?
misconceptions: Multiplies u by y · u without dividing by u · u
Gives the residual y − p, the part left after projecting
Thinks a vector projects onto any line unchanged

questions.prompt: A data analyst's feature matrix has five columns. Its singular values are 2951, 89.6, 32.9, 6.0 and 0. What does the zero tell her?
options: One column is an exact combination of the others, so the matrix has rank 4
The fifth column is all zeros
The fifth feature is unimportant for prediction
The matrix has only four rows
questions.explanation: A zero singular value means a direction the columns cannot reach: one column is a linear combination of the others.
misconceptions: Reads a zero singular value as a zero column; it marks a dependent direction
Confuses a zero singular value with a weak predictor
Reads rank as the number of rows rather than independent directions

questions.prompt: A covariance matrix of three features has eigenvalues 4.0, 0.9 and 0.1. What share of the variance lies along the first principal component?
questions.explanation: Variance shares are eigenvalue / sum of eigenvalues: 4.0 / 5.0 = 0.80.
misconceptions: Reads the eigenvalue itself as a percentage
Assumes each of the three components holds an equal share
Adds the shares of the first two components

questions.prompt: In link ranking with damping, the second-largest eigenvalue has size 0.85. The error of power iteration therefore shrinks by about 0.85 at each step.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Power iteration's error falls by the ratio |λ₂| / |λ₁| each step, and λ₁ = 1 here.
misconceptions: Thinks the speed of power iteration depends on the largest eigenvalue alone

questions.prompt: The search lead wants to store a ratings matrix at low rank and asks how much error each rank would leave. Which quantity answers that directly?
options: The rank of the matrix
The determinant of the matrix
The singular values after the k-th: their squares sum to the squared error of the best rank-k copy
The largest eigenvalue of the covariance matrix
questions.explanation: By Eckart-Young, ‖A − A_k‖²_F = σ²ₖ₊₁ + … + σ²ₙ, so the tail of the singular values gives the error.
misconceptions: Thinks the rank alone says how much a rank-k copy loses
Expects one number to describe the error at every rank; it is not even defined for a non-square matrix
Uses only the first component, which says nothing about the tail that is dropped

questions.prompt: A least-squares fit fails with 'Singular matrix'. One column is total actions, which is the exact sum of three other columns. What fixes it?
options: Rescale every column to unit variance
Add more rows of the same kind
Switch to 32-bit floats
Drop one of the dependent columns, so the remaining columns are independent
questions.explanation: The columns are exactly dependent, so XᵀX is singular whatever the scale or number of rows; removing the redundant column restores full rank.
misconceptions: Thinks scaling breaks an exact linear dependency; it does not
Expects more data to help; every new row keeps the same dependency
Thinks the failure is about precision rather than an exact dependency

questions.prompt: If cond(X) is 2,213, then cond(XᵀX) is about 4.9 million.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Forming XᵀX squares the condition number: 2,213² ≈ 4.9 × 10⁶.
misconceptions: Thinks XᵀX has the same condition number as X

questions.prompt: Two features are nearly collinear. Refitting on a slightly different sample swings their coefficients from +0.4 to −1.3, yet the predictions barely change. What is happening?
options: The system is ill-conditioned: the data fix the sum of the two effects, not each one separately
The solver has a bug
The model needs more features
The predictions must be wrong too
questions.explanation: Near-collinear columns leave a direction the data barely constrain: coefficients move along it while the fitted values hardly change.
misconceptions: Expects a correct solver to give stable coefficients on any data
Thinks adding columns helps; near-collinear columns make it worse
Assumes unstable coefficients imply unstable predictions

questions.prompt: In 64-bit arithmetic both QR and the normal equations give a coefficient of 0.4228. In 32-bit arithmetic the normal equations give 0.4308. What is the most likely cause?
options: The true coefficient is 0.4308 and 64-bit arithmetic hides it
Rounding error amplified by the squared condition number of XᵀX
A different random seed
QR is only an approximation
questions.explanation: In 32-bit floats the relative error is about 10⁻⁷ times cond(XᵀX) ≈ 5 × 10⁶, enough to change the second decimal.
misconceptions: Trusts the less precise result over the more precise one
Looks for randomness in a deterministic computation
Thinks QR is approximate; it is exact in exact arithmetic

questions.explanation: Multiplying on the right by this B swaps the columns of A.
misconceptions: Computes B A, which swaps the rows; matrix products do not commute
Multiplies entry by entry instead of rows by columns
Gives the transpose of A

questions.prompt: What is the inverse of [[2, 1], [1, 1]]?
questions.explanation: The determinant is 1, so the inverse is [[d, −b], [−c, a]] = [[1, −1], [−1, 2]]; check: the product is I.
misconceptions: Inverts each entry separately
Swaps the diagonal but forgets to negate the off-diagonal entries
Gets the sign of the whole matrix wrong

questions.prompt: What are the singular values of the diagonal matrix [[3, 0], [0, −4]]?
options: 4 and 3
3 and −4
−4 and 3
7 and 1
questions.explanation: Singular values are the square roots of the eigenvalues of AᵀA = diag(9, 16), listed largest first: 4 and 3.
misconceptions: Thinks singular values can be negative and keep the diagonal's order
Sorts by value but keeps the sign
Adds and subtracts the diagonal entries

questions.prompt: A and B are NumPy arrays of shape (3, 4). Which expression gives the 3 × 3 matrix of dot products between the rows of A and the rows of B?
options: A @ B
A @ B.T
A * B
A.T @ B
questions.explanation: Row i of A times column j of Bᵀ (row j of B) is entry (i, j): (3, 4) @ (4, 3) gives (3, 3).
misconceptions: Forgets that inner dimensions must match: (3, 4) @ (3, 4) fails
Uses the element-wise product, which keeps the shape (3, 4)
Takes dot products between columns, giving a 4 × 4 matrix

questions.prompt: With X = Q R (Q has orthonormal columns, R is upper triangular), which system gives the least-squares coefficients β?
options: β = Qᵀ y
Rᵀ β = Q y
R β = Qᵀ y
XᵀX β = Qᵀ y
questions.explanation: Xᵀ X β = Xᵀ y becomes Rᵀ R β = Rᵀ Qᵀ y, and R is invertible, so R β = Qᵀ y, solved by back substitution.
misconceptions: Forgets the triangular factor R
Transposes the wrong factors
Mixes the normal equations with the QR right-hand side

questions.prompt: On nearly dependent columns, modified Gram-Schmidt keeps Q as orthogonal as Householder QR does.
options: True
False
